To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
chronic exposure to indinavir (an HIV-protease inhibitor) exacerbates the diabetic state in Zucker diabetic fatty (ZDF) fa/fa rats and dramatically exacerbates hyperglycemia in ZDF rats.
chronic exposure to the HIV-protease inhibitor IDV in male ZDF rats exacerbated insulin resistance and diabetes and induced the suppressor of cytokines signaling-1 signaling cascade.
HIV-PIs induce the SOCS- 1 signaling cascade in insulin-sensitive tissues, resulting in insulin resistance and diabetes in Zucker diabetic fatty rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which HIV-PIs induce insulin resistance and diabetes.
the molecular mechanisms by which HIV-PIs induce insulin resistance, diabetes, and other metabolic abnormalities.

the molecular mechanisms that contribute to the pathophysiological changes that occur in HIV-positive patients exposed chronically to HIV-PI therapy, which include insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, and type II diabetes mellitus.

the PI indinavirexacerbates diabetes mellitus in ZDF rats by inducing SOCS-1 and that this effect may contribute to the metabolic syndrome associated with chronic PI treatment in humans

the HIV-protease inhibitor (PI) indinavir (IND) accelerates and exacerbates the diabetic state in male Zucker diabetic rats (ZDF), compared with vehicle-treated rats, and that IND induces suppressor of cytokines signaling-1 (SOS-1) signaling, an inducer of insulin and glucose intolerance, in insulin-sensitive tissues.

HIV protease inhibitors (PI), in addition to their well-known direct inhibitory action against HIV, also have indirect effects on the host metabolism, which may contribute to the development of insulin resistance, diabetes, and dyslipidemia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-PIs promote insulin resistance and diabetes in part through induction of the SOCs-1 signaling pathway.
the SOCS-2 signaling cascade is induced by HIV-PIs and that this is an important factor in the development and progression of metabolic dysregulations associated with long-term HIV-PI exposure.

The main takeaway from our work is that

HIV-protease-inhibitor (PI) exposure induces the suppressor of cytokines signaling-1 (SOS-1) signaling cascade, which is an established mechanism for insulin resistance and type II diabetes mellitus, in both insulin-sensitive tissues and cultured cell models.

HIV-protease inhibitor (PI) exposure can induce the expression of suppressor cytokine signaling- 1 (SOCS1) in insulin sensitive tissues of Zucker diabetic fatty rats and that this induction of SOCS1 is likely a major contributor to the development of metabolic dysfunction in HIV-positive patients treated with PIs for long periods of time.
HIV protease inhibitors can induce insulin resistance and diabetes in vivo, in a rodent model.
